title: Raindrops aren't teardrop-shaped
hook: Falling raindrops look less like teardrops and more like hamburger buns.
peek: The classic teardrop shape is a myth. Small raindrops are nearly round, and bigger ones flatten underneath as air pushes on them, until the largest burst apart into smaller drops on the way down.
lede: Draw a raindrop and you will probably draw a teardrop, pointed at the top. Real falling raindrops never look like that. Surface tension pulls small drops into near-perfect spheres. As drops grow, the air rushing past pushes their undersides flat, so a large raindrop looks more like the top half of a hamburger bun than a tear.

bullets.text: The pointed shape belongs to a drop clinging to a tap or a leaf, stretched by its own weight just before it lets go. Once a drop falls free, surface tension quickly pulls it round.
Drops much bigger than about 5 millimetres across rarely survive the fall. The air flattens them into a cup that balloons into a thin bag, which then bursts into a spray of smaller drops.
Wilson Bentley, better known for photographing snowflakes, measured raindrops in the early 1900s. He let them fall into trays of flour and measured the little dough pellets they formed.
Scientists study falling drops by holding them in an upward stream of air inside a vertical wind tunnel. High-speed cameras show the drops wobbling and flattening just as they would in a real fall.
